question: Which of the following statements about the role of the intestine in development of obesity best describes the situation?
options: Obesity occurs because gut hormone secretion becomes deranged and PYY secretion fails to give a satiety signal.
The gut/brain signalling pathway controls energy intake to within 2% of requirements, even in people who are morbidly obese
The problem is one of greed and gluttony, whereby people override strong satiety signals on a regular basis
Flavour signals from tasty, processed food will override satiety signals even after a large meal
model_outputs: Options B, C and D sound unsatisfying because of their extreme emphasis. D suggests the dominating role of flavour signals in overly processed foods, while C suggests the dominating role of overactive appetite in some people. B is equally unconvincing in light of recent widely published evidence that people increasingly are unable to control homing energy needs through homeostatic (hunger and satiety) mechanisms. This leaves us with option A. "Obesity occurs because gut hormone secretion becomes deranged and PYY secretion fails to give a satiety signal" as the most appealing explanation. Research with mice, humans and our primate cousins, the great apes, has defined a scientific basis for this new concept of obesity that "the problem starts in the gut", as well as pioneering new treatments for obesity, including a new satiety-mimetic drug PYY-(3-36) that is currently under development and will be able to take advantage of the intuitive link between leaky gut and obesity in new ways. The answer is (A).

question: A 40-year-old man with paranoid schizophrenia is transferred to the emergency department from the residential facility where he lives 2 hours after having swallowed a nail. The patient says he does not have any symptoms. Medical history is otherwise unremarkable. His only current medication is haloperidol. The patient is not in acute distress. Vital signs are normal. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status examination discloses a flat affect, distractibility, and derailment of thoughts. X-ray of the abdomen is obtained and shows a 4-cm nail in the left upper quadrant. No free air is visible. After admitting the patient to the hospital, which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Open laparotomy and removal of the nail through a gastrotomy incision
Insertion of a nasogastric tube to suction out the nail
Administration of activated charcoal to bind the nail and facilitate its removal
Removal of the nail through endoscopic esophagogastroscopy
Administration of a barium swallow to track the nail's passage
Administration of ipecac to induce vomiting and expectoration of the nail
Administering a laxative to expedite the passage of the nail
Observation to allow passage of the nail via normal peristalsis
Use of a magnet to draw out the nail
model_outputs: The nail is located in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen, suggesting it is in the stomach. The patient's mental health condition, paranoid schizophrenia, and the method of ingestion do not immediately suggest gastrointestinal symptoms. Medical knowledge dictates that in cases of swallowed foreign bodies (such as a nail), the initial approach generally involves observation if the object is located in the stomach or duodenum, and the patient shows no signs of complications like gastrointestinal bleeding or obstruction. Given that the patient is not in acute distress and the X-ray shows no free air (no perforation), it is appropriate to adopt a wait-and-see approach. Endoscopy for removal in a non-urgently symptomatic case is typically not the first step unless complications arise, as many ingested sharp objects can pass through the gastrointestinal tract without invasive intervention. Therefore, allowing the nail to pass via normal peristalsis is reasonable. The answer is (H).

question: Which virus infection was not first identified by clinical observation?
model_outputs: HIV, the causative agent of AIDS, was first identified in the early 1980s when doctors in the United States reported several uncommon infections in otherwise healthy young men. Rubella teratogenicity (causing congenital rubella syndrome) was identified through clinical observations of birth defects and developmental issues in infants born to mothers who had rubella during pregnancy. The link between Zika virus and microcephaly was also identified by observing clinical cases where pregnant women infected with Zika gave birth to infants with unusually small heads and significant brain damage. Hepatitis C, however, was first identified not through clinical observation but through molecular techniques. It was discovered in 1989 when Dr. Michael Houghton and his team at Chiron Corporation used cloned viral cDNA to identify the virus in the sera of blood donors, leading to the first detection of the Hepatitis C virus (HCV) by the identification of HCV RNA. It was a laboratory discovery rather than an initial clinical observation. The answer is (D).

question: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus passes blood from the
options: pulmonary vein to the pulmonary artery.
pulmonary artery to the pulmonary vein.
model_outputs: We refer to Wikipedia articles on anatomy for help. Let’s solve this problem step by step. A major respiratory shunt existing in the fetal circulation is called the ductus arteriosus, which is also known as DA. It is a vital part of fetal circulation connecting the pulmonary artery, that will be connected to the lungs once the newborn starts to breathe and bring oxygen to the pediatric body, and the descending aorta, where it allows a much-desired movement of blood away from the fetal lungs. As the oxygenation of blood is provided by the placenta and not the lungs, the ductus arteriosus is a unique structure because it allows the pulmonary flow of blood from the right ventricle. The ductus arteriosus relies on the blood vessel that regulates its opening and closing. The ductus arteriosus is closed — that’s its function in newborns — by oxygen-rich blood from the lungs. One interesting fact about the ductus arteriosus is that if it doesn’t close quickly — perhaps to days or weeks after birth — serious damage to the heart, lungs and brain can result. As we can see, the answer choice (C) is the only correct answer to this question. The answer is (C).

question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 2-hour history of confusion and agitation. He also has had fever, headache, stiff neck, and vomiting since he returned from summer camp 2 days ago. His parents say he does not use illicit drugs. On arrival, he is combative and there is evidence of hallucinations. His temperature is 40°C (104°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 17/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. A lumbar puncture is performed. Results of cerebrospinal fluid analysis show cysts and trophozoites. The most likely portal of pathogen entry into this patient's central nervous system is which of the following?
model_outputs: The symptoms described—confusion, agitation, fever, headache, stiff neck, vomiting, combative behavior, hallucinations, and the presence of cysts and trophozoites in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) point towards a diagnosis of primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, most likely caused by Naegleria fowleri. This amoeba typically enters the body through the nasal cavity and travels to the central nervous system via the olfactory nerve. Therefore, the most likely portal of entry for the pathogen into the central nervous system is the olfactory nerve. The answer is (D).

question: The coronary arteries

model_outputs: We refer to Wikipedia articles on anatomy for help. According to the article, the coronary arteries are two large blood vessels (the left and the right coronary arteries) that supply blood to the heart muscle itself, and they arise from the ascending aorta. We also know that the ventricles relax during diastole, which allows the coronary arteries involved in supplying the ventricles to fill. Blood normally flows through the ventricular myocardium during diastole; hence, coronary blood supply 90% occurs during diastole. The major part of the coronary arteries fill with blood during diastole, complementing the systolic filling of the coronary arteries located near the bases of the aorta. The answer is (I).

question: A 67-year-old woman comes to the physician because of easy bruising for 4 months. She has a history of lung cancer treated with radiation therapy 6 months ago. question: A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of mild nausea, increased urinary urgency and frequency, and constipation. She also has had a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the past 2 weeks and a 3-week history of vaginal bleeding. Pelvic examination shows a nodular cervix with an irregular, friable posterior lip, and a rock-hard, irregular, immobile pelvic mass that extends across the pelvis. Transactivation of cellular growth factor genes by TAX
model_outputs:
This patient presents with a cervical mass likely due to cervical cancer, as evidenced by the biopsy results indicating well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, common in the cervix. One significant cause of cervical cancer is human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. HPV contributes to cancer pathogenesis by integrating its viral DNA into the host genome and expressing E6 and E7 oncoproteins. These viral oncoproteins bind and inactivate tumor suppressor proteins: p53 and Rb, respectively. Inactivation of the tumor suppressor protein p53 by the HPV E6 protein disrupts normal cell cycle control, contributing to carcinogenesis by allowing the accumulation of mutations and genomic instability.

Therefore, the pathogenesis of the patient's disease involves the inactivation of cellular p53. The answer is (A).

question: A previously healthy 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department in August 1 hour after the onset of headache, dizziness, nausea, and one episode of vomiting. Immerse the patient in an ice water bath

model_outputs:
We have a 15-year-old boy with symptoms of headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, high body temperature, tachycardia, tachypnea, orthostatic hypotension, and altered mental status. These symptoms are indicative of heatstroke, which is a medical emergency.

The most critical initial step in managing heatstroke is rapid cooling to reduce body temperature, along with stabilizing hemodynamics. The preferred method is immersion in an ice water bath, as it is the most effective way to quickly lower core temperature.

The answer is (D) Immerse the patient in an ice water bath.
